Gauge boson. Gauge bosons, also called vector bosons, are spin-one bosons that mediate fundamental forces through gauge symmetry principles. The photon carries electromagnetism, the W and Z bosons mediate the weak force, and gluons mediate the strong force. Their masslessness or mass is linked to their respective gauge symmetries—broken symmetry can generate mass, as in electroweak theory.

The photon is a massless gauge boson that couples to electric charge and has infinite range. Gluons are eight massless carriers of color charge that mediate the strong force. The W bosons are massive, each with an energy of eighty giga-electron-volts, and mediate charged-current weak decays. The Z boson is also massive at ninety-one giga-electron-volts and mediates neutral-current weak interactions. Gauge symmetry determines interaction properties: unbroken symmetry yields massless particles, while broken symmetry yields massive ones. Each gauge boson couples with a strength determined by its coupling constant—the fine-structure constant for the photon and the strong coupling constant for gluons.

Gauge bosons are the foundation of the Standard Model's force framework. The unification of electromagnetism and weak force through electroweak symmetry predicted the massive W and Z bosons decades before their experimental discovery. The theory's predictive power—predicting masses, decay widths, and coupling strengths—was spectacularly confirmed, validating the gauge principle as a guiding law of nature governing all fundamental forces.
